Under the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 and procedural provisions of the BNSS, granting probation (either upon admonition or on entering into a bond of good conduct) is entirely a matter of judicial discretion. The court must consider the circumstances of the case, the nature of the offence, and the character and antecedents of the offender before deciding whether probation is appropriate instead of a sentence of imprisonment.
Does every section of the Indian Penal Code map one-to-one to the exact same section number in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?

No, this premise is false. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) does not maintain the section numbering of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The BNS completely restructured and consolidated criminal offences into 358 sections (compared to 511 in the IPC). For instance, murder, which was defined under Section 300 and punished under Section 302 of the IPC, is now governed under Section 101 and Section 103 of the BNS. Assuming identical section numbers between IPC and BNS is a fundamental legal error.
Does every cyber offence in India fall under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act?

No, this premise is incorrect. Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is a specific provision dealing exclusively with 'identity theft'—the fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password, or other unique identification feature. The IT Act contains distinct provisions for other cyber offences, such as hacking and data damage (Section 43 read with Section 66), receiving stolen computer resources (Section 66B), cheating by personation (Section 66D), privacy violations (Section 66E), cyber terrorism (Section 66F), and publishing obscene material (Section 67). Not all cyber offences fall under Section 66C.
Is an oral agreement completely void and unenforceable under Indian contract law?

No, the premise that all oral agreements are void is incorrect. Under Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement is a valid contract if it is made by free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and is not expressly declared to be void. The law does not require all contracts to be in writing; oral agreements are legally valid and binding unless a specific statute explicitly mandates that a particular category of contract must be in writing and registered (such as transfer of immovable property under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or arbitration agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996).
Does entering into an unregistered Agreement to Sell make the buyer the legal owner of immovable property in India?

No, this premise is legally false. Under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an Agreement to Sell does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on immovable property; it is merely an executory contract promising to transfer ownership in the future. Legal ownership of immovable property valued at one hundred rupees or more can only be transferred through a duly stamped and registered Sale Deed executed in accordance with Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908.
Can an employer in India terminate any employee at will without notice or severance pay?

No, this assumption is incorrect. Indian labour and employment law does not follow the doctrine of unbridled 'employment at will'. Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, State Shops and Commercial Establishments Acts, and applicable service rules, termination of non-managerial employees (workmen) requires mandatory statutory notice (or pay in lieu of notice), retrenchment compensation, and compliance with statutory procedures, unless termination is for proved misconduct following a domestic inquiry.
Does the term 'non-bailable offence' mean that bail can never be granted under any circumstances?

No, that is a common misconception. In Indian criminal procedure, a 'non-bailable offence' does not mean that bail is prohibited. Rather, it means that bail cannot be claimed as a matter of absolute right from the police or the court (unlike in bailable offences). In non-bailable cases, the grant of bail is a matter of judicial discretion exercised by the court under statutory principles, considering the gravity of the offence, likelihood of absconding, and risk of tampering with evidence.
Is adultery currently a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment in India?

No, this premise is outdated. In the landmark judgment *Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018)*, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court struck down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code (which criminalized adultery) as unconstitutional, holding that it violated Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution. Adultery is no longer a criminal offence in India, although it remains recognized as a civil ground for divorce under personal matrimonial statutes.
Are all arbitration awards in India final and immune from any court challenge?

No, this premise is incorrect. While the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 promotes party autonomy and minimal judicial intervention, arbitral awards are not completely immune from challenge. Under Section 34 of the Act, an aggrieved party can apply to a court to set aside an award on specific limited grounds, such as incapacity of a party, invalidity of the arbitration agreement, violation of natural justice, or where the award is in conflict with the public policy of India or vitiated by patent illegality.
Does the registration of a First Information Report (FIR) prove the accused person's guilt?

No, this premise is legally erroneous. An FIR is not substantive evidence of the accused's guilt. It is merely the initial information recorded by police under procedural law to set the criminal investigative machinery in motion. An accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt through admissible evidence presented at a judicial trial.
Are consumer disputes in India prosecuted as criminal trials under the Indian Penal Code?

No, that premise is incorrect. Consumer disputes are civil, regulatory, and compensatory matters adjudicated under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 before quasi-judicial Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (District, State, and National). They are not criminal trials conducted under penal codes, although penal enforcement mechanisms exist under Section 72 of the Consumer Protection Act for non-compliance with Commission orders.
Can Parliament amend any part of the Constitution of India without any limitation under Article 368?

No, this assumption is incorrect. While Parliament has wide constituent power to amend the Constitution under Article 368, that power is subject to the fundamental limitation established by the Supreme Court in the landmark *Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)* ruling: Parliament cannot alter, damage, or destroy the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution (such as democracy, rule of law, judicial review, secularism, and federalism).
Is a confession made to a police officer admissible as conclusive evidence of guilt in an Indian court?

No, this premise is contrary to Indian evidence law. Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (and earlier under Sections 25 and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872), confessions made to a police officer are strictly inadmissible in evidence against the person making them, subject only to the limited discovery of fact rule. This statutory bar protects accused persons against coerced or involuntary custodial confessions.
Does an Indian passport holder automatically lose their Indian citizenship upon purchasing real estate abroad?

No, purchasing real estate or property abroad has no effect on Indian citizenship. Under Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, an Indian citizen only loses their citizenship if they voluntarily acquire the citizenship or nationality of another foreign country, as India does not permit dual citizenship.
Are all agreements in restraint of trade valid if entered into between consenting adults?

No, this premise is false. Under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void, subject to a narrow statutory exception relating to the sale of the goodwill of a business. Consenting to a void restraint of trade clause does not make it legally enforceable.
Does a woman lose all rights to maintenance upon divorce in India?

No, this premise is false. Under Indian law, a divorced woman is legally entitled to claim maintenance from her former husband under various statutory frameworks—including Section 125 CrPC / Section 144 BNSS, personal divorce laws (such as Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act), and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act—until she remarries or is otherwise disentitled by law.
Can a police officer conduct an arrest in all cases without obtaining a magistrate's warrant?

No, this assumption is incorrect. Police can only arrest without a warrant in 'cognizable offences' where statutory preconditions (such as reasonable suspicion or credible information of serious crime) are met under procedural law. In 'non-cognizable offences', police have no legal power to arrest without a warrant issued by a competent magistrate.
Does copyright in a literary work in India require mandatory registration to be legally protected?

No, this premise is incorrect. Under the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright protection arises automatically upon the creation and fixation of an original work in tangible form; registration with the Copyright Office is voluntary and serves as prima facie evidence in court, but is not a mandatory prerequisite for acquiring copyright or suing for infringement.
Is a company's director personally liable for all civil contractual debts of the company?

No, this premise is legally false. Under the principle of corporate personality established in *Salomon v. Salomon* and recognized under the Companies Act, 2013, a company is a separate legal entity distinct from its directors and shareholders. Directors are not personally liable for company debts unless they have executed personal guarantees, committed fraud, or the corporate veil is pierced by a court.
Does silence always constitute acceptance of an offer under the Indian Contract Act?

No. Under general principles of Indian contract law established in *Felthouse v. Bindley*, mental acceptance or mere silence does not constitute valid acceptance. Acceptance of a proposal must be communicated to the proposer in an external manifestation, unless the course of dealing or statute implies acceptance by conduct under Section 8 of the Indian Contract Act.
Can an Indian citizen file a Fundamental Rights petition directly in the Supreme Court for breach of an ordinary contract by a private company?

No, this premise is incorrect. Writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution for enforcement of Fundamental Rights lie against the 'State' as defined under Article 12, not against purely private commercial entities for breach of private contract. Ordinary commercial breaches must be pursued through civil suits or arbitration.
Does every criminal case in India require a preliminary inquiry before an FIR can be registered?

No. Under the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench decision in *Lalita Kumari v. Govt of UP (2014)*, registration of an FIR is mandatory if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. A preliminary inquiry is permissible only in a narrow set of specified categories (such as medical negligence, matrimonial disputes, commercial disputes, corruption allegations, or cases with abnormal delay) to ascertain whether a cognizable offence is disclosed.
Can a tenant acquire ownership of rented property merely by paying rent continuously for 20 years?

No, this assumption is completely unfounded. A tenant occupying property under a lease or tenancy agreement acknowledges the landlord's title. Under the principle of tenant estoppel (codified in evidence law) and established property jurisprudence, permissive possession as a tenant can never ripen into adverse possession or ownership, regardless of the duration of occupancy.
Is every homicide in India automatically classified and punished as murder?

No. Indian penal law maintains a clear distinction between 'culpable homicide' (the genus) and 'murder' (the species). All murders are culpable homicides, but not all culpable homicides amount to murder. If an act falls within statutory exceptions (such as grave and sudden provocation, exercise of private defence in good faith, or sudden fight in the heat of passion), it is punished as culpable homicide not amounting to murder, carrying a lesser sentence.
Can an FIR be registered only at the police station in whose local jurisdiction the crime took place?

No, that premise is incorrect. Under Indian criminal procedure, a 'Zero FIR' can be lodged at any police station regardless of territorial jurisdiction when information of a cognizable offence is received; the police station must register the information, assign it a Zero serial number, initiate immediate preliminary steps if necessary, and transfer it to the jurisdictional police station for formal investigation.
Does the death of the complainant automatically abate all criminal proceedings?

No, this premise is false. In cognizable state-prosecuted offences, the state represents the public interest, and the death of the original informant or victim does not automatically terminate the prosecution. In private complaint cases, courts have discretion under procedural law to permit legal heirs or interested parties to continue the prosecution.
Are all government notifications valid immediately even if not published in the Official Gazette?

No. As held by the Supreme Court in *Harla v. State of Rajasthan*, legal rules, orders, and subordinate legislation must be promulgated and published in the Official Gazette to have the force of law. Secret or unpublished administrative decrees cannot impose legal obligations or penal consequences on citizens.
Does filing a civil suit automatically stay criminal proceedings arising from the same transaction?

No. It is well-established law that civil and criminal proceedings arising out of the same facts can proceed concurrently. A civil dispute regarding property or contractual breach does not automatically stay a criminal prosecution for fraud or forgery, unless a competent court specifically grants a stay to prevent abuse of process.
Is an unregistered gift deed of agricultural land legally valid in India?

No. Under Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908, a gift of immovable property must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses. An unregistered gift of immovable land transfers no title.
Can a father disinherit his son from his ancestral coparcenary property by writing a simple will?

No, this premise is incorrect. Under Hindu succession law, a person can only dispose of their 'separate or self-acquired property' and their undivided interest in coparcenary property by will; they cannot unilaterally disinherit coparceners from the entire joint ancestral coparcenary estate in which other coparceners have acquired rights by birth.
Does a post-dated cheque mean that the issuer cannot be prosecuted under Section 138 of the NI Act?

No. Once the date written on a post-dated cheque arrives, it becomes a valid negotiable instrument payable on demand. If presented within its validity period and dishonoured for insufficient funds, Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act applies fully upon service of statutory notice and non-payment.
Are all medical negligence allegations in hospitals automatically treated as criminal offences?

No. The Supreme Court in *Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005)* clarified that to attract criminal liability under penal law, the negligence of a medical doctor must be 'gross negligence', not mere error of judgment or ordinary civil negligence compensable under tort or consumer law.
Does the right to information under the RTI Act extend to confidential cabinet discussions before a decision is taken?

No. Under Section 8(1)(i) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, Cabinet papers, including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries, and other officers, are exempt from disclosure until the decision has been taken and the matter is complete or over.
Can an Indian High Court grant divorce under its writ jurisdiction under Article 226?

No. Divorce is a statutory civil remedy that must be sought through petitions filed before competent Family Courts or District Courts under applicable personal laws. Article 226 writ jurisdiction is meant for constitutional and public law remedies, not for dissolving private marriages.
Does an acquittal in a criminal case automatically entitle the person to a job with the government?

No. An acquittal from a criminal charge merely removes the bar of criminal conviction; it does not confer an automatic constitutional right to appointment. Government recruitment remains subject to fitness, character verification, and merit eligibility rules.
Is an arbitration clause automatically rendered void if the main commercial agreement is terminated for breach?

No, this premise is false. Under the doctrine of severability (codified in Section 16(1) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996), an arbitration clause is treated as an independent agreement that survives the termination, breach, or invalidity of the main contract.
Can an Indian citizen hold a valid trademark without ever using it in commerce?

While a trademark can be registered based on 'proposed to be used', maintaining a trademark requires bona fide commercial use. Under Section 47 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a registered trademark can be taken off the register upon application by an aggrieved person if it was registered without bona fide intention to use or has not been used continuously for five years.
Is payment of dowry legally valid if both families agree to it in writing?

No, this premise is completely false. Under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, both giving and taking dowry are illegal, void, and cognizable criminal offences. An agreement between families to give or take dowry is void ab initio under Section 5 of the Act and does not provide a legal defence.
Why is it essential for an AI legal assistant to identify and challenge false premises in user queries?

It is essential because user questions often incorporate inaccurate legal assumptions, fabricated section numbers, or misunderstood doctrines. If an AI assistant uncritically accepts a false premise, it generates legally flawed, misleading, or hallucinated responses. Challenging and clarifying the premise first ensures that the subsequent legal explanation is accurate, grounded in verified law, and helpful to the user.

An elderly father gifted his residential property to his son on the condition that the son would look after him, but the son has now abandoned and mistreated him. Which specific statute provides the most effective legal remedy to cancel the gift deed?

The most direct and specialized statute is the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007. Under Section 23 of this Act, where a senior citizen has transferred property by gift or otherwise subject to the condition that the transferee shall provide basic amenities and physical needs, and the transferee fails or refuses to do so, the transfer of property is deemed to have been made by fraud, coercion, or undue influence, and can be declared void by the Maintenance Tribunal. This summary statutory remedy is far faster and more accessible than filing a protracted civil suit.
A business customer's payment cheque was returned with the bank memo 'insufficient funds'. Which primary statute governs the legal notice and criminal complaint for this dishonour?

The primary statute is the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, specifically Section 138. Under this special enactment, the payee must issue a statutory demand notice in writing within 30 days of receiving the memo from the bank, giving the drawer 15 days to pay. If payment is not made within 15 days of receiving the notice, a formal criminal complaint must be filed before the competent Judicial Magistrate within one month thereafter. General criminal provisions for cheating under BNS/IPC do not substitute for this special statutory procedure unless fraudulent intent existed at the very inception of the transaction.
A woman faces domestic abuse and harassment in her matrimonial home and requires an urgent order restraining her husband from evicting her. Which statute provides this emergency civil remedy?

The governing statute is the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA). Under Sections 18 and 19 of the PWDVA, a Magistrate can grant urgent 'protection orders' and 'residence orders' prohibiting the respondent from committing domestic violence, entering the aggrieved person's place of employment, or evicting her from the shared household, regardless of whether she has any legal title in that property. These civil remedies operate independently of and in addition to any criminal prosecution.

A homebuyer paid 90% of the purchase price for an apartment, but the builder has delayed handover by two years beyond the agreed completion date. Which specific statute provides for refund with interest or monthly delay compensation?

The primary and specialized enactment is the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA). Under Section 18 of RERA, if a promoter fails to give possession in accordance with the terms of the agreement for sale, the allottee has the right to withdraw from the project and demand a full refund of the amount paid along with interest at the prescribed rate, or, if the allottee chooses not to withdraw, to receive monthly interest compensation for every month of delay until possession is handed over. Remedies before Consumer Commissions under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 are also concurrently available.
A 14-year-old child was subjected to sexual assault. Which specialized penal statute takes precedence in prosecuting this offence?

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 takes precedence. The POCSO Act is a dedicated special statute designed to protect children (defined as any person below 18 years) from offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography. By virtue of Section 42A, the POCSO Act has overriding effect over general penal law, incorporates statutory presumptions of culpable mental state (Section 29 and 30), and mandates trial before designated Special Courts with child-friendly procedures.
A consumer purchased a new refrigerator that stopped working within two weeks, and both the seller and manufacturer refuse repair or replacement. Which statute governs the complaint?

The governing statute is the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The aggrieved buyer can file a consumer complaint alleging 'deficiency in service', 'defect in goods', and 'unfair trade practice' before the competent District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under Section 34/35, seeking replacement, refund, and compensation for mental agony and financial loss.
A tech employee stole confidential source code and customer databases from their employer's servers using an unauthorized USB device. Which specialized statute applies?

The Information Technology Act, 2000 is the primary specialized statute governing this conduct. Under Section 43 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, unauthorized downloading, copying, or extracting of data from any computer resource is a statutory offence attracting civil liability for compensation as well as criminal imprisonment and fines. Additionally, general penal provisions for theft and criminal breach of trust under BNS may be invoked concurrently.

Two corporate entities have a commercial dispute regarding the supply of industrial machinery under an agreement containing an arbitration clause. Which statute regulates the appointment of the arbitrator?

The governing statute is the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Under Section 11 of this Act, if the parties fail to agree on the appointment of an arbitrator in accordance with their contract, an application may be made to the High Court (for domestic arbitrations) or the Supreme Court (for international commercial arbitrations) for the appointment of an independent arbitrator.

An individual wants to challenge a state government notification that directly violates their Fundamental Right to equality under Article 14. What is the appropriate constitutional forum and mechanism?

The individual can file a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the competent State High Court, or directly before the Supreme Court of India under Article 32. These constitutional writ remedies enable the higher judiciary to issue directions, orders, or writs (such as certiorari or mandamus) quashing unconstitutional executive notifications.

A supplier delivered goods under a commercial contract, but the buyer refused to pay the agreed contract price without justification. Under which statute does the supplier sue for the debt and contractual damages?

The supplier initiates a civil suit for recovery of money and damages under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (governing performance of contracts and compensation for breach under Section 73) read with the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (action for the price under Section 55) and the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 if the dispute meets the specified commercial pecuniary threshold.
A bank customer was tricked by an imposter pretending to be a bank official who obtained their OTP and transferred funds online. Which cyber law provision specifically applies to this personation?

Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 specifically penalizes 'cheating by personation by using computer resource'. It applies directly where a person by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personating another, punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine. This is accompanied by general criminal charges of cheating and fraud under BNS/IPC.
A registered proprietor discovers that a rival company is selling counterfeit shoes bearing their exact registered brand logo. Which statute provides the primary civil and criminal remedies?

The primary statute is the Trade Marks Act, 1999. Under Section 29, the proprietor can file a civil suit for trademark infringement seeking an injunction, delivery up of infringing goods, and damages or an account of profits. Additionally, Section 103 and 104 of the Act prescribe criminal penalties for applying false trademarks or selling goods with false trade descriptions.
An individual seeks copies of government inspection reports and file notings regarding public road construction. Which statute applies?

The Right to Information (RTI) Act, 2005 is the governing statute. Under Section 6 of the RTI Act, any Indian citizen can file a formal application with the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the concerned public authority, seeking access to public records, inspection of works, and certified copies, subject only to the specific exemptions under Section 8.
A person who was arrested claims they were tortured during police custody. Which legal provisions establish the procedural framework for medical examination and inquiry?

Under procedural law in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) (formerly Sections 53, 54, and 176 of the CrPC), an arrested person has the statutory right to be medically examined by a medical officer upon arrest and remand. Furthermore, in cases of custodial violence, custodial death, or custodial rape, a mandatory judicial inquiry by a Judicial Magistrate is prescribed.
A software company wishes to protect its newly developed proprietary software algorithm from being copied. Which IP statute primarily protects computer source code in India?

Computer source code and object code are primarily protected as 'literary works' under the Copyright Act, 1957 (Section 2(o)). Patent protection under the Patents Act, 1970 is generally excluded for a 'computer programme per se' under Section 3(k), unless the software demonstrates a technical contribution or technical effect working in combination with specialized hardware.

A borrower defaults on a secured commercial bank loan, and the bank wants to seize and auction the mortgaged commercial property without waiting for a lengthy civil suit. Which statute enables this summary recovery?

The governing statute is the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002. Under Section 13 of the SARFAESI Act, a secured creditor (bank or financial institution) can enforce its security interest against mortgaged property without the intervention of a civil court, following the issuance of a 60-day statutory demand notice and possession procedures.
A company is unable to pay its operational debts of Rs. 1.5 Crores to an operational creditor. Which statute governs the insolvency resolution process?

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) is the specialized enactment. An operational creditor can initiate a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) under Section 9 of the IBC before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), provided the default exceeds the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore and statutory demand notice requirements under Section 8 are satisfied.
A landlord seeks to evict a commercial tenant for non-payment of rent in a metropolitan city. Which legal framework applies?

The matter is governed by the state-specific Rent Control or Tenancy Act (such as the Delhi Rent Control Act, Maharashtra Rent Control Act, or Tamil Nadu Regulation of Rights and Responsibilities of Landlords and Tenants Act) or the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Sections 106 and 111) if the property is exempt from rent control, requiring formal termination of tenancy by notice before instituting an eviction suit before the competent Rent Authority or Civil Court.
A seller sells agricultural land to a buyer using an unregistered agreement and receives full payment. The seller now refuses to execute the sale deed. What is the buyer's primary remedy?

The buyer's primary civil remedy is to file a suit for specific performance of the contract under the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as amended in 2018, which made specific performance of contracts a general statutory entitlement rather than a purely discretionary relief), seeking a court decree directing the seller to execute and register the formal Sale Deed.
A hospital administered expired medication to a patient during surgery, causing severe complications. Which statutory forums can the patient approach?

The patient can approach: (1) The Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for medical negligence and compensation; (2) The National Medical Commission / State Medical Council for disciplinary action against the medical practitioners; and (3) In cases of gross, reckless negligence, initiate criminal proceedings under penal law.
A citizen was denied a passport without any written reason or hearing. Which enactment regulates passport refusal and appeals?

The Passports Act, 1967 is the governing enactment. Under Sections 5, 6, and 7, the passport authority must record reasons for refusing a passport and communicate them to the applicant (unless exempted on grounds of national security), and the aggrieved person has a statutory right of appeal under Section 11 to the designated appellate authority.
A female employee alleges that her supervisor made sexually suggestive remarks and demanded sexual favours at the workplace. Which specialized enactment applies?

The governing enactment is the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (commonly known as the POSH Act). Under this Act, the employer must have an Internal Committee (IC) to conduct a time-bound inquiry into the complaint, provide interim relief, and submit inquiry recommendations, in addition to any criminal remedies under penal law.

A contractor fails to finish public road repairs by the contract deadline. The contract contains a liquidated damages clause specifying Rs. 10,000 per day of delay. Which statute governs the enforcement of this clause?

Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs the enforcement of liquidated damages clauses. Under Section 74 (and established rulings such as *Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass* and *Kailash Nath Associates*), the court will award reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount stipulated, and the named sum operates as a ceiling rather than an automatic penalty.
A dispute arises regarding the custody of a 6-year-old child between separated Hindu parents. Which statute governs the custody application?

Child custody between Hindu parents is governed primarily by the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 read with Section 13 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, which establishes the foundational legal principle that the 'welfare of the child' is the paramount consideration.
A person was subjected to an unlawful search and seizure of their mobile device by customs officers at an international airport. Which statute governs customs searches?

The Customs Act, 1962 is the governing statute. Under Sections 100, 102, and 105 of the Customs Act, officers have specific statutory powers of search and seizure of persons, goods, and conveyances, subject to procedural safeguards such as the right of the person to be taken before a gazetted officer or magistrate upon request.
An aggrieved party claims that an arbitral tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction and made an order without hearing them. Which statute and section provide for setting aside the award?

The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is the governing statute, specifically Section 34. Section 34(2) provides the exclusive statutory grounds for setting aside an arbitral award, including lack of proper notice, inability to present one's case, or where the award deals with a dispute not contemplated by the submission to arbitration.
A manufacturer falsely advertised that its health supplement 'cures diabetes in 7 days'. Under which statute can the Central Consumer Protection Authority take suo motu action?

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) takes action under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Under Sections 18, 19, and 21 of the Act, the CCPA has the statutory power to investigate misleading advertisements, issue directions to discontinue or modify them, and impose penalties up to ten lakh rupees on manufacturers and endorsers.
An individual seeks probate of a registered will executed by their deceased father. Which statute regulates the grant of probate and letters of administration?

The Indian Succession Act, 1925 is the governing enactment. Under Part IX of the Indian Succession Act (Sections 217–315), petitions for grant of probate or letters of administration are filed before the competent District Court or High Court exercising testamentary jurisdiction.
A commercial establishment employed children aged 12 to work in a restaurant. Which specialized statute strictly prohibits this employment?

The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 is the primary statute. Following the 2016 amendments, the Act completely prohibits the employment of a child (below 14 years of age) in any occupation or process whatsoever (with narrow family-enterprise exceptions outside school hours), and makes violation a cognizable and non-bailable criminal offence.

A resident's neighbour operates an unlicensed commercial welding workshop in a residential apartment, generating dangerous smoke and noise. Which summary preventive criminal procedure can the magistrate invoke?

The Executive Magistrate can invoke summary preventive proceedings for the removal of public nuisance under procedural law in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) (formerly Section 133 of the CrPC), by issuing a conditional order directing the removal of the nuisance or cessation of the commercial trade within a specified time.
An employee was dismissed without receiving statutory gratuity after 7 years of continuous service. Which enactment governs the payment and recovery of gratuity?

The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is the specialized enactment. Under Section 4, an employee who has rendered continuous service for not less than five years is entitled to gratuity upon termination of employment. In case of non-payment, the employee can approach the Controlling Authority appointed under Section 7 of the Act.
A person received offensive and threatening voice messages on WhatsApp from an anonymous number. Which statutes provide remedies?

The matter involves both the Information Technology Act, 2000 (for transmitting offensive or threatening digital communications and cheating/impersonation if false identities are used) and the substantive penal provisions under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (criminal intimidation and insulting the modesty of a woman where applicable), investigated under the BNSS.

A minority shareholder alleges that majority shareholders in a private company are siphoning corporate funds and managing company affairs in an oppressive manner. Which statute and forum provide relief?

The Companies Act, 2013 is the governing statute. Under Sections 241 and 242 of the Act, qualifying shareholders can file an application alleging 'oppression and mismanagement' before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), which possesses wide powers to regulate the conduct of the company's affairs, alter articles, or remove directors.
An author claims that a publishing house printed and sold 5,000 copies of their novel without paying royalties or obtaining a written license. Which statute applies?

The Copyright Act, 1957 applies. Under Section 19, an assignment or license of copyright must be in writing and signed, and under Section 55, the author can institute a civil suit for copyright infringement seeking an injunction, recovery of royalties, damages, and rendition of accounts.
A property buyer discovers that the seller had already mortgaged the land to a cooperative bank before executing the sale agreement. Which statute protects the bank's prior charge?

The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (under the doctrine of prior mortgage and Section 48 regarding priority of rights created by transfer) and the Registration Act, 1908 (giving notice of registered encumbrances to the public) protect the bank's prior registered mortgage, rendering the subsequent purchaser's rights subject to the bank's security interest.
A private bus collided with an auto-rickshaw, severely injuring a passenger. Which specialized tribunal adjudicates compensation for death or bodily injury in motor accidents?

The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) established under Chapter XII of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is the specialized forum. Under Sections 165 and 166 of the Act, claims for compensation arising out of motor accidents are filed before the MACT on principles of fault or structured no-fault formulas against the driver, owner, and insurance company.
A consumer's flight was cancelled without prior notification, leaving them stranded without alternative transport or refund. Which regulatory body and rules govern passenger compensation?

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR Section 3 - Air Transport, Series M, Part IV) read with the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 govern passenger rights, mandating compensation for cancelled or delayed flights, alternative flights, meals, and refunds.
A husband and wife married under Hindu rites want to dissolve their marriage by mutual consent after two years of living separately. Which statute and section apply?

The application is filed under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Under Section 13B, both spouses can jointly petition the Family Court for divorce by mutual consent upon establishing that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more and have mutually agreed to dissolve the marriage.
An inventor developed a novel, inventive mechanical valve for industrial pumps. Under which statute do they apply for exclusive monopoly rights for 20 years?

The inventor applies under the Patents Act, 1970. Under Section 2(1)(j), a patent may be granted for an invention that is new, involves an inventive step (non-obviousness), and is capable of industrial application, conferring an exclusive right of commercial exploitation for a term of 20 years from the filing date.
A builder constructs an extra floor in violation of approved municipal building plans. Which authority and statute regulate demolition or compounding of unauthorized building work?

The relevant State Municipal Corporation or Town and Country Planning Act (such as the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 or Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966) governs unauthorized construction, granting the municipal commissioner statutory authority to issue stop-work notices, order demolition, or compound minor non-structural infractions.

A complainant wants to initiate criminal contempt against an individual who published a defamatory article scandalizing the authority of a High Court. Which statute regulates criminal contempt proceedings?

The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 regulates contempt proceedings. Under Section 15 of the Act, criminal contempt of a High Court can be initiated by the court on its own motion (suo motu) or on a motion brought by the Advocate General, or by any other person with the written consent of the Advocate General.
An individual wants to change their name across all official identification records (PAN, Aadhaar, Passport). Which legal procedure is followed in India?

The standard legal procedure involves: (1) Executing an affidavit before a notary or executive magistrate declaring the name change; (2) Publishing a name-change notification in two prominent newspapers (one in English, one in the regional language); and (3) Publishing a formal notification in the official Gazette of India (Department of Publication), which is then submitted to update identity registries.
A worker in a factory lost their fingers during machine operation due to lack of safety guards. Which statute provides statutory compensation without requiring proof of employer negligence?

The Employee's Compensation Act, 1923 (formerly the Workmen's Compensation Act) provides structured statutory compensation for occupational injuries and disablement arising out of and in the course of employment, adjudicated by the Commissioner for Employee's Compensation on a no-fault liability basis.
A company fails to hold its mandatory Annual General Meeting (AGM) within the prescribed statutory period. Under which enactment can a shareholder apply for directions to convene the meeting?

Under Section 97 of the Companies Act, 2013, if a company fails to hold its annual general meeting within the statutory time limit, any member of the company may apply to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), which has the statutory power to direct the calling and holding of an AGM.
A shopkeeper is selling adulterated food products endangering public health. Which specialized regulatory enactment applies alongside penal law?

The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA) is the comprehensive regulatory statute. It establishes the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) and prescribes administrative inspections, sample testing, seizure powers, and civil and criminal penalties for manufacturing, storing, or selling unsafe or adulterated food articles.
A dispute arises regarding who owns a parcel of land when both parties claim ownership through unregistered partition deeds. Which statute governs the admissibility of unregistered partition deeds?

The Registration Act, 1908 (Section 17 and Section 49) read with the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 governs this issue. A partition deed that creates, declares, or extinguishes rights in immovable property requires mandatory registration; if unregistered, Section 49 bars it from affecting property or being received as evidence of any transaction affecting such property, save for collateral purposes.
A state electricity board disconnected a consumer's power supply arbitrarily without issuing a statutory notice of disconnection. Which specialized forum can the consumer approach?

The consumer can approach the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (CGRF) established under Section 42(5) of the Electricity Act, 2003, and subsequently the Electricity Ombudsman, or approach the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for deficiency in service.
A foreign national is found residing in India after the expiry of their visa without valid extension. Which statute governs deportation and penalties for unauthorized stay?

The Foreigners Act, 1946 read with the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920 regulates the entry, stay, and departure of foreigners. Under Section 14 of the Foreigners Act, remaining in any area in India without valid authority beyond the permitted period is a cognizable criminal offence, and the Central Government possesses the statutory authority to order deportation.

A commercial contract contains a clause stating that 'any dispute shall be referred to arbitration in London under English law'. If an interim relief application is needed to freeze assets in India, which statute applies?

Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 applies. Following the 2015 amendments to Section 2(2), Indian courts have jurisdiction under Section 9 to grant interim relief to preserve assets or evidence located in India even in international commercial arbitrations seated outside India, unless the parties have expressly excluded Section 9.
Why is it essential to identify the governing legal enactment before citing specific section numbers?

Identifying the governing statute first is essential because Indian law is organized into specialized enactments (such as the IT Act for cyber offences, RERA for real estate disputes, NI Act for cheques, PWDVA for domestic violence civil relief, and POCSO for child sexual abuse) that have specific statutory procedures, standards of proof, and designated tribunals. Attempting to force specialized disputes into general penal provisions (like BNS) or civil code provisions leads to incorrect legal advice and ineffective procedural remedies.
Which section of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 governs the admissibility of electronic records in court?

Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), the admissibility of electronic and digital records is governed primarily by Section 63 (alongside Sections 61 and 62), which replaces Section 65B of the repealed Indian Evidence Act, 1872. Section 63 sets out the conditions under which an electronic record printed on paper, stored, recorded, or copied in optical or magnetic media is deemed to be a document and admissible in evidence, accompanied by a certificate as specified in the Schedule. It is a common error to refer to 'Section 65B' in the context of the BSA.
Is there a 'Section 65B' in the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023?

No. Section 65B was a provision of the repealed Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) is a completely re-enacted statute with a new structure consisting of 170 sections. The legal principles governing the admissibility of electronic and digital records and certificate requirements are codified under Section 63 of the BSA, not under a section named 65B.
How many sections does the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 contain compared to the old Indian Evidence Act, 1872?

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) contains exactly 170 sections divided into 12 chapters and a Schedule. In contrast, the repealed Indian Evidence Act, 1872 contained 167 sections. Because the sections have been restructured and consolidated, one cannot assume that a section number from the 1872 Act corresponds to the same number in the 2023 BSA.
Does the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam recognize electronic and digital records as documents?

Yes. Under Section 2(1)(d) and Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), electronic and digital records are explicitly included within the definition and category of 'documents'. The BSA provides that nothing in the Act shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic record in evidence on the sole ground that it is an electronic record, subject to compliance with the standards laid down in Section 63.
Why is it a legal error to cite 'Section 65B(4) of the BSA' when tendering electronic evidence?

It is a legal error because Section 65B(4) was the subsection in the old Indian Evidence Act, 1872. In the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, the requirement for an electronic evidence certificate (specifying the particulars, device management, and integrity of the electronic output) is codified under Section 63 and its accompanying Schedule. Citing Section 65B in a trial conducted under BSA reveals reliance on repealed statutory numbering.
Are confessions made to police officers admissible under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam?

No. The fundamental exclusionary rule barring confessions made to police officers from being proved against a person accused of an offence is preserved under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) (formerly Section 25 of the 1872 Act). Statements made to police officers while in custody remain inadmissible in court as confessions, maintaining essential safeguards against coerced self-incrimination.
What is the equivalent in the BSA of the discovery of fact rule under Section 27 of the old Evidence Act?

The discovery of fact doctrine—where information given by an accused in police custody leads to the discovery of a distinct physical fact, weapon, or article—is codified within the confession provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA). Only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered is admissible in evidence.
How does the BSA treat primary and secondary evidence of documents?

Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the court, while secondary evidence includes certified copies, copies made from the original by mechanical processes, counterparts of documents, and oral accounts of the contents of a document. As a general rule, documents must be proved by primary evidence, except under specified statutory conditions where secondary evidence is permitted.
Can an AI system cite Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act as the governing law in an ongoing 2025 trial?

No. In a trial governed by current law in 2025, the court applies the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA). Statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses (including dying declarations) are now governed by the corresponding provisions of the BSA, not the repealed 1872 Act.
What is the statutory certificate requirement for electronic evidence under Section 63 of the BSA?

Under Section 63(4) of the BSA, any person seeking to produce an electronic record in court must provide a certificate identifying the electronic record, describing the manner in which it was produced, giving particulars of the device involved in its production, and certifying that the computer or device was operating properly without interference during the relevant period, signed by a person in official charge or management of the device.
Did the BSA introduce a Schedule for electronic record certification?

Yes. Unlike the old Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 includes a formal Schedule setting out the standardized format for the certificate to accompany electronic records, specifying details of the device, data integrity, and hash values where applicable.
Under which statute are judicial notices of foreign law and Indian statutes taken by courts today?

Judicial notice of facts—including all laws in force in India, public Acts passed by Parliament, and the accession of foreign states—is taken by courts under the provisions of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), relieving parties of the need to formally prove undisputed public enactments.
Can oral evidence be given to contradict the terms of a written registered contract under the BSA?

No. The exclusionary rule that when the terms of a contract, grant, or other disposition of property have been reduced to the form of a document, no oral evidence shall be admitted to contradict, vary, add to, or subtract from its terms is preserved in the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), subject to narrow exceptions like fraud, illegality, or failure of consideration.
How does the BSA define an 'expert'?

Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), an expert is a person specially skilled in foreign law, science, art, handwriting, finger impressions, or digital and electronic evidence, whose opinion becomes a relevant fact when the court has to form an opinion upon any of those specialized points.
Does the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam govern the competency of a child witness?

Yes. Under the BSA, all persons are competent to testify unless the court considers that they are prevented from understanding the questions put to them, or from giving rational answers to those questions, by reason of tender years, extreme old age, disease of body or mind, or any other cause. A child witness is competent if they understand the duty of speaking the truth.
In a trial under the BSA, who carries the burden of proof in an alibi defence?

Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), while the general burden of proving the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt rests on the prosecution throughout, the specific burden of proving the plea of alibi (that the accused was elsewhere at the time of the crime) rests on the accused under the rule that whoever asserts a fact must prove it.
What is the danger of automatically mapping old Evidence Act section numbers to the BSA?

The danger is that the BSA is not a simple re-print of the 1872 Act; sections have been renumbered, definitions modernized (particularly for digital records), obsolete colonial terms removed, and new procedural requirements (like the certificate Schedule) incorporated. Blindly using 1872 numbers leads to citing repealed sections and submitting legally defective pleadings.
Does the BSA allow leading questions during cross-examination?

Yes. Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), leading questions (questions suggesting the answer which the person putting it wishes or expects to receive) may be asked freely in cross-examination, whereas in examination-in-chief and re-examination they cannot be asked without the permission of the court if objected to by the adverse party.
Can an unregistered document be admitted as secondary evidence under the BSA if the law requires registration?

Generally no. If a document is required by law to be registered (such as a mortgage or sale of immovable property under Section 17 of the Registration Act), failure to register it bars it from being admitted in evidence to affect the property, and secondary evidence cannot be used to circumvent the mandatory statutory bar of registration, except for proving collateral transactions.
Summarize the golden rule for citing evidence law provisions in India today.

The golden rule is: For all proceedings governed by the current law, cite the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA), verify the exact section number within its 170-section framework (such as Section 63 for electronic records instead of old Section 65B), and avoid projecting repealed section numbers of the 1872 Indian Evidence Act into modern court proceedings.
A hacker gains unauthorized access to a hospital's patient database, deletes medical records, and introduces ransomware. Which IT Act provision specifically applies to this hacking and data damage?

This conduct falls squarely under Section 43 read with Section 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 43 covers civil liability for unauthorized access, downloading, damage, disruption, or denial of access to computer systems, while Section 66 criminalizes any act referred to in Section 43 done dishonestly or fraudulently, punishing it with imprisonment up to three years, or fine up to five lakh rupees, or both. It should not be mislabeled as Section 66C (which is identity theft).

A fraudster creates a fake social media profile using a celebrity's name and photographs to deceive followers into donating money to a private bank account. Which specific cyber provision applies to this cheating by personation?

This offence is governed by Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which specifically punishes 'cheating by personation by using computer resource'. Under Section 66D, whoever by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personating another is punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine up to one lakh rupees. While the profile creation involves misrepresentation, the act of using it to fraudulently extract money is personation cheating under 66D (alongside general cheating under BNS/IPC), not mere identity theft under 66C.

An individual fraudulently obtains another person's net-banking password and digital signature certificate and uses them to access their account. Which specific IT Act section penalizes identity theft?

This specific conduct is penalized under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which defines and punishes 'identity theft'. Section 66C applies where someone fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person, punishable with imprisonment up to three years and fine up to one lakh rupees. Section 66C applies to the misappropriation and unauthorized use of digital identifiers.
A landlord secretly installed a hidden camera inside a female tenant's bathroom and captured private videos. Which IT Act provision specifically penalizes this violation of bodily privacy?

This conduct is specifically penalized under Section 66E of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which addresses 'violation of privacy'. Section 66E makes it an offence to intentionally or knowingly capture, publish, or transmit the image of a private area of any person without their consent, under circumstances violating privacy, punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or fine up to two lakh rupees, or both.

A group of hackers compromises the critical computer network of the national power grid and disrupts electric supply to threaten the security and sovereignty of India. Which specialized cyber provision applies?

This conduct constitutes 'cyber terrorism' under Section 66F of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Section 66F applies when someone, with intent to threaten the unity, integrity, security, or sovereignty of India or to strike terror in people, denies authorized access to critical computer systems or accesses protected computer resources. It is a grave non-bailable offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to life imprisonment.
Explain the key difference between Section 66C and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act.

The key distinction lies in the nature of the criminal act: Section 66C penalizes 'identity theft'—the mere fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's unique electronic identity (such as a password, PIN, electronic signature, or biometric identifier). In contrast, Section 66D penalizes 'cheating by personation using a computer resource'—where the offender actively pretends to be someone else (or adopts a fictitious character) to induce a victim to part with property or money. In short, 66C is unauthorized use of an identity token, whereas 66D is active deceit and fraud through personation.
A person knowingly buys a stolen high-end laptop that was illegally taken from a software company's office. Which IT Act section specifically penalizes receiving stolen computer resources?

This offence is governed by Section 66B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which penalizes 'dishonestly receiving stolen computer resource or communication device'. Whoever dishonestly receives or retains any stolen computer resource or communication device, knowing or having reason to believe it to be stolen, is punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or with fine up to one lakh rupees, or with both.
Why is it legally incorrect to cite Section 66C for all forms of hacking, data deletion, and phishing?

It is legally incorrect because the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides distinct statutory provisions for distinct cyber conducts: hacking and system damage fall under Section 43 read with Section 66; data theft/stolen hardware falls under 66B; identity theft falls under 66C; phishing and online cheating fall under 66D; privacy violations fall under 66E; and cyber terrorism falls under 66F. Using Section 66C as a blanket answer for all cybercrimes ignores statutory categorization and misstates the legal charge.
An individual uploads sexually explicit videos of an adult without their consent on an internet portal. Which IT Act provisions apply?

This conduct falls under Section 67A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which specifically penalizes publishing or transmitting material containing sexually explicit acts in electronic form (punishable on first conviction with imprisonment up to five years and fine up to ten lakh rupees), alongside Section 66E for privacy violation if captured without consent, and Section 67 for general obscenity.
A social media platform is sued because an anonymous user posted defamatory content about a politician. What statutory defense does the platform claim?

The social media platform claims the statutory 'safe harbour' protection available to intermediaries under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Under Section 79 (and the Supreme Court ruling in *Shreya Singhal v. Union of India*), an intermediary is not liable for third-party information, data, or communication links hosted by it, provided it observes due diligence under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 and expeditiously removes access upon receiving an order from a competent court or government agency.
A cyber criminal sends bulk phishing emails disguised as an official tax refund notification to trick taxpayers into entering banking credentials on a cloned website. Which cyber provisions apply?

This conduct involves multiple distinct offences: (1) Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 for cheating by personation; (2) Section 66 of the IT Act read with Section 43 for unauthorized access and extraction of data; and (3) substantive criminal charges of forgery, fraud, and cheating under the BNS/IPC. It should not be restricted solely to Section 66C.
What is the statutory punishment under Section 66F of the IT Act for cyber terrorism?

Under Section 66F(2) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, whoever commits or conspires to commit cyber terrorism is punishable with imprisonment which may extend to imprisonment for life. It is the most severe criminal penalty provided under the IT Act.
Does the IT Act contain provisions regarding the liability of company directors for cyber offences committed by a corporate entity?

Yes. Under Section 85 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, where a contravention of any of the provisions of the Act has been committed by a company, every person who at the time of the contravention was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of its business, as well as the company itself, is deemed to be guilty of the contravention and liable to be proceeded against, unless they prove it occurred without their knowledge or that they exercised all due diligence.
An ex-employee sends automated Denial of Service (DoS) traffic to overwhelm an e-commerce website during a festive sale. Which section applies?

This conduct falls under Section 43(f) read with Section 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which specifically prohibits denying or causing the denial of access to any person authorized to access any computer resource. When done dishonestly or fraudulently, it is a criminal offence under Section 66.
Under which IT Act section are computer viruses, malware, and trojans prohibited?

Introducing or causing to be introduced any computer contaminant or computer virus into any computer, computer system, or computer network is prohibited under Section 43(c) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and is made a punishable criminal offence under Section 66 when done dishonestly or fraudulently.
A person circulates child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on an online chat group. Which enactments govern the prosecution?

The prosecution is governed primarily by Section 67B of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (which specifically criminalizes browsing, downloading, creating, or transmitting child sexual abuse material electronically, carrying severe imprisonment up to five years on first conviction) read with the specialized provisions of Section 13, 14, and 15 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012.
Can a person be prosecuted under both the Information Technology Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for the same online fraud?

Yes. The Supreme Court has held (such as in *State of UP v. Aman Mittal* and *Sharat Babu Digumarti*) that where the ingredients of a general penal offence (like cheating, forgery, or criminal breach of trust under BNS/IPC) and a special cyber offence under the IT Act (like Section 66D) are made out, both enactments can be invoked, provided the accused is not punished twice for the exact same statutory ingredient in violation of Article 20(2) of the Constitution.
Which authority in India is empowered to issue blocking orders for web pages or apps under the IT Act?

Under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Central Government (through the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, MeitY) has the statutory authority to issue directions to block public access to any computer resource in the interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defense of India, security of the State, or public order, following the procedural safeguards prescribed under the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009.
A telecom store employee steals SIM cards registered in a customer's name to bypass OTP security. Which cyber law provision applies?

The fraudulent acquisition and misuse of digital credentials and identification features fall under Section 66C of the IT Act (identity theft) and Section 66D (cheating by personation) if used to defraud, alongside substantive criminal charges of theft and criminal breach of trust under BNS/IPC.
Summarize the golden rule for answering cyber-law questions under the Information Technology Act.

The golden rule is: Categorize the specific nature of the digital misconduct before citing provisions. Use Section 43/66 for hacking, malware, and system disruption; Section 66B for stolen hardware/resources; Section 66C for password/digital signature identity theft; Section 66D for online cheating and personation; Section 66E for bodily privacy violations; Section 66F for cyber terrorism; Section 67/67A/67B for obscene content/CSAM; and Section 79 for intermediary safe harbour. Never default to Section 66C for all cyber matters.
